question: Adenine on a ribose with three phosphates in a row makes _____, the molecule a cell spends whenever it needs a reaction driven the wrong way.
questions: A human body hydrolyses between 100 and 150 moles of _____ a day, which is far more than it contains at any moment and shows how fast the molecule is remade.
Restoring the ion balance after one nerve impulse costs a neuron close to a billion molecules of _____, which is where most of the brain's energy goes.
abstract:
ATP, adenosine triphosphate, is the principal form of chemical energy inside cells, and it is a nucleotide: an adenine base on a ribose sugar carrying three phosphate groups bonded one after another. Removing the outermost phosphate gives ADP, and that hydrolysis is energetically favourable, which is what lets a cell couple it to reactions that would not otherwise run. The metaphor of a currency is apt because the molecule is spent and remade rather than stored, and a human body hydrolyses somewhere between 100 and 150 moles of it in a day. The bill falls hardest on tissues that pump ions, and a neuron hydrolyses close to a billion molecules to reset its sodium and potassium after a single depolarisation. Other nucleotides do similar work, carrying energy or reactive chemical groups through a wide range of metabolic reactions.

Energy is not the whole of what ATP does, and it is co-stored and co-released with neurotransmitters, which makes it a mediator of purinergic signalling in the nervous system. Released from damaged cells it becomes a warning: in the liver, extracellular ATP acts on neighbouring and on its own cells as a signal in the progression of fibrosis. A third role has nothing to do with either, since at the concentrations found inside a cell ATP alters how proteins interact with one another and how stable they are. That effect is being examined on proteins which cluster into droplets, where ATP and other small amphiphilic molecules tune how those clusters form. A molecule known for a century as the cell's fuel is turning out also to be part of how its interior stays soluble.
